boundaries.evidence: The definition admits the empty root system and the zero series: the sums over an empty Φ+ are zero, the convolution over an empty support has all coefficients 0, and e^0 remains the unit, exactly as recorded in the definition.

The zero series is the additive identity with empty support; the convolution formula gives all coefficients 0, so the coefficient bounds and the ring axioms hold trivially in this instance. The case is recorded in the statement.

Rank one is the first nontrivial instance: with a single simple root the convolution coefficient at η is bounded by the single coordinate of λi+μj−η, which is exactly the finiteness argument in the definition.

Degenerate supports collapsing to one downward cone, including the point case λ−{0} of finite support, are inside the stated family; the product of two downward cones is again a downward cone by additivity of Q+, the closure step used in the definition.

boundaries.reason: A downward cone is a translation of the closed monoid Q+; there is no interval endpoint or first/last exponent for an axis to attach to.

boundaries.evidence: No selection from a family of nonempty sets occurs: the data Φ+, P and the cones are fixed, and the only quantification is over coefficients; the definition inherits no Choice obligation.

boundaries.reason: The item fixes notation for a ring; it asserts no equivalence of two conditions, so no forward direction of a biconditional is claimed.
Nothing in the definition denies a converse of the convolution formula; there is simply no converse statement to discharge here.

risk_review.notes: Definition: simple-root coordinate boxes make every convolution coefficient finite; the analogous three-factor box justifies associativity, and product support lies in finitely many summed cones. Arbitrary h* cone translations do not change this argument. Zero series, rank zero, finite support, and e^0 are valid. Opened root-system conventions, category-O character definition and Verma character statement; MIT §26.2 supplies the integral-lattice specialization. No analytic convergence or Weyl action on arbitrary completed series is inferred.

boundaries.evidence: A finite-dimensional module may be zero: its weight set is empty, the sum over the empty set of weights is the zero series, and the definition returns ch 0 = 0 with no nonzero coefficient to bound.

The zero functional is an allowed weight and the zero module has only the zero coefficient family; the definition registers m_λ(ν)=0 for any ν that is not a weight, so this instance follows from the definition itself.
The trivial one-dimensional module has exactly one weight, the zero weight with multiplicity one, so its character is the single term e^0; the finite sum of the definition covers it.

Weight spaces are permitted to be zero or one-dimensional without further hypotheses; the definition imposes no positivity or dominance condition on the weights, so degenerate multiplicity patterns such as a two-point weight set are included.

boundaries.reason: The character is a finite unordered sum over weights; no interval, truncation parameter or limiting index occurs, so there are no endpoints to inspect.

boundaries.evidence: The definition assumes the Axiom of Choice through the cited decomposition of a finite-dimensional module; the finite weight sum itself requires only finite choice.

boundaries.reason: The definition names a formal object; it postulates no equivalence with a separate condition, so no forward implication of an iff exists.
There is no converse direction: the item does not claim that an arbitrary coefficient family is a module character, only that characters give such families.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module, where $\mathfrak g$ is a
finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra
$\mathfrak h$, and let
$$V=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}V_\mu$$
be its weight-space decomposition, with $V_\mu$ the weight space of
[[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]
([[prop-finite-dimensional-representations-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra-decompose-into-weight-spaces]]).
The **formal character** of $V$ is
$$\operatorname{ch}V:=\sum_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}(\dim V_\mu)e^\mu\in\mathcal R,$$
the finite sum with integer coefficients taken in the completed formal
character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]; equivalently,
$\operatorname{ch}V$ is the coefficient family $\mu\mapsto\dim V_\mu$ on
$\mathfrak h^*$, which has finite support by the cited decomposition.

We write
$$m_\lambda(\mu):=\dim L(\lambda)_\mu$$
for the multiplicity of $\mu$ as a weight of the finite-dimensional simple
module $L(\lambda)$ of highest weight $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$
([[thm-highest-weight-classification-of-finite-dimensional-irreducible-representations]]),
so that $\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=\sum_\mu m_\lambda(\mu)e^\mu$; the
coefficients $m_\lambda(\mu)$ are nonnegative integers and
$m_\lambda(\mu)=0$ for all but finitely many $\mu$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For the abelian category [[thm-category-o-is-abelian-and-extension-closed]], define $K_0(\mathcal O)$ as the free abelian group on isomorphism classes $[M]$, modulo $[B]=[A]+[C]$ for every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$. A set of representatives suffices: every finitely generated $U(\mathfrak g)$-module is a quotient of some $U(\mathfrak g)^n$, and those quotients form a set up to isomorphism.

Define the formal character by $\operatorname{ch}M=\sum_\mu(\dim M_\mu)e^\mu$. By [[prop-equivalent-support-description-of-category-o]], its integer coefficients are finite and supported in finitely many downward cones. Let $\mathscr R$ be the group of all such integer coefficient families, with pointwise addition. It is a ring with $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$: at a fixed resulting weight, in any pair of cones the equation $\beta+\gamma=\eta$ with $\beta,\gamma\in Q^+$ has finitely many solutions, since every simple-root coefficient is bounded. Taking weight spaces is exact, so character gives a well-defined homomorphism $K_0(\mathcal O)\to\mathscr R$. The zero object's class and character are zero.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

Every Verma module $M(\lambda)$, every quotient of it, and every finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module belongs to $\mathcal O$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

If $E$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module, the functor $M\mapsto E\otimes_{\mathbb C}M$ with diagonal action is exact and maps $\mathcal O$ into itself.

Let $(V_i)_{i\in I}$ be representations of $\mathfrak g$, and let $V,W$ be
representations. Then the following formulas define representations:

$$x(v_i)_{i\in I}=(xv_i)_{i\in I},$$

$$ (x\lambda)(v)=-\lambda(xv),$$

$$ (xT)(v)=xT(v)-T(xv),$$

$$x(v\otimes w)=xv\otimes w+v\otimes xw,$$

on $\bigoplus_iV_i$, $V^*$, $\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,W)$, and $V\otimes_kW$,
respectively.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra with a fixed Cartan
subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ ([[def-cartan-subalgebra-of-a-lie-algebra]]), and let
$V$ be a representation of $\mathfrak g$
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]), written $H\cdot v$ for
$\rho(H)(v)$. No finite-dimensionality of $V$ is assumed here.

For $\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ the **weight space** of $\mu$ is
$$V_\mu=\{v\in V:H\cdot v=\mu(H)v\text{ for every }H\in\mathfrak h\};$$
this is a linear subspace of $V$
([[def-linear-subspace]]), being the intersection of the kernels of the
endomorphisms $\rho(H)-\mu(H)\operatorname{id}_V$. A **weight** of $V$ is a
functional $\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ with $V_\mu\ne0$, and a nonzero $v\in V_\mu$
is a **weight vector** of weight $\mu$. The zero functional is allowed as a
weight; $V_0$ is the space of vectors fixed by $\mathfrak h$.

Distinct weight spaces are independent. Indeed, if
$v_1+\dots+v_m=0$ with $0\ne v_j\in V_{\mu_j}$ and pairwise distinct functionals
$\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m$, choose $H\in\mathfrak h$ with the scalars $\mu_j(H)$
pairwise distinct; this is possible because the finitely many sets
$\{H\in\mathfrak h:(\mu_i-\mu_j)(H)=0\}$ are proper subspaces of $\mathfrak h$
(the functionals $\mu_i-\mu_j$ are nonzero for $i\ne j$) and a finite union of
proper subspaces of a vector space over the infinite field $\mathbb C$ is
proper. Then the $v_j$ are eigenvectors of $\rho(H)$ for the
pairwise distinct eigenvalues $\mu_j(H)$ and hence are linearly independent
([[thm-eigenvectors-for-distinct-eigenvalues-are-linearly-independent]]),
forcing $v_1=\dots=v_m=0$, a contradiction. Thus the sum
$\sum_\mu V_\mu$ is direct.

If $V$ is finite-dimensional, then $V$ has only finitely many weights: the
nonzero weight spaces form a direct sum inside $V$, so their number is at most
$\dim V$.

Fix the finite Weyl root-system data of
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]: the real span
$E$ of the roots with its positive definite form, a positive system $\Phi^+$
with base $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, the root group
$Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha\subseteq P$, the weight lattice
$P\subseteq E$, and the positive cone
$$Q_+=\sum_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$$
(the set written $Q^+$ in
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]). A **downward cone**
is a set $\lambda-Q_+=\{\lambda-\beta:\beta\in Q_+\}$ with
$\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$.

The **completed formal character ring** $\mathcal R$ is the set of formal sums
$$f=\sum_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}c_\mu e^\mu,\qquad c_\mu\in\mathbb Z,$$
whose support $\operatorname{supp}f=\{\mu:c_\mu\ne0\}$ is contained in a
finite union of downward cones. Addition is coefficientwise, the product is
the convolution
$$(fg)_\eta=\sum_{\mu+\nu=\eta}c_\mu d_\nu,$$
and the unit is $e^0$, so that $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$. The product is
well defined: if $\operatorname{supp}f$ lies in
$\bigcup_{i=1}^m(\lambda_i-Q_+)$ and $\operatorname{supp}g$ in
$\bigcup_{j=1}^n(\mu_j-Q_+)$, then a pair of exponents contributing to $\eta$
lies in some $\lambda_i-Q_+$ and some $\mu_j-Q_+$, and the solutions
$\beta,\gamma\in Q_+$ of $\beta+\gamma=\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta$ are the elements
of the box $0\le\beta_k\le(\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta)_k$ in the simple-root
coordinates, a finite set (empty unless $\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta\in Q_+$). The
coefficients are integers, and a finite union of downward cones is again such
a union, so addition and multiplication make $\mathcal R$ a commutative
$\mathbb Z$-algebra. In the notation of
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]] this is the ring
denoted $\mathscr R$ there, where the character homomorphism of category
$\mathcal O$ takes its values; the elements of finite support form the group
ring $\mathbb Z[\mathfrak h^*]$ of the additive group $\mathfrak h^*$ and
contain the subring $\mathbb Z[P]$ generated by the $e^\mu$ with
$\mu\in P$.

By [[prop-formal-character-of-a-verma-module]],
$$\operatorname{ch}M(\lambda)=e^\lambda\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$$
is an element of $\mathcal R$: the geometric series
$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha}$ is supported in the downward cone $-Q_+$, and a
finite product of elements of $\mathcal R$ lies in $\mathcal R$ by the
convolution formula, while $e^\lambda$ is a single monomial. **No convergence
of any formal sum is asserted**: all sums are formal, coefficients are
compared coefficientwise, and every finite sum, product or finite product of
geometric series below is interpreted in $\mathcal R$ by the rules just
recorded.

derivations.claim: By [F2] each $\mathfrak g$-linear map of $\mathfrak h$-semisimple modules restricts to the weight spaces, and the short exact sequence of the statement restricts to the short exact sequence $0\to V'_\mu\to V_\mu\to V''_\mu\to0$ for every $\mu$, so the dimensions satisfy $\dim V_\mu=\dim V'_\mu+\dim V''_\mu$; moreover [F3] describes the weight spaces of a tensor product as the direct sum over $\mu+\nu=\eta$ of the tensor products of the weight spaces.

u=\eta}V_\mu\otimes W_
u$, so $\dim(V\otimes W)_\eta=\sum_{\mu+
u=\eta}(\dim V_\mu)(\dim W_
u)$; the argument of step 2.1, now applied to these coefficients, gives $\operatorname{ch}(V\otimes W)=\sum_\eta igl(\sum_{\mu+
u=\eta}(\dim V_\mu)(\dim W_
u) igr)e^\eta=(\operatorname{ch}V)(\operatorname{ch}W)$ by the convolution rule of [F4].

boundaries.evidence: The zero module and a zero tensor factor are the empty cases: step 2.1 records ch 0 = 0 and step 3.1 then gives ch(V⊗0)=0=ch V·ch 0, using the empty weight set of the zero module.
When Vμ is the zero space the dimension identity of step 1.1 reads 0=0+0, and the multiplicativity statement of step 3.1 is unaffected because the zero space contributes no terms to the convolution.

One-dimensional modules and one-factor tensor products are the first nontrivial instance: ch C = e^0 is the unit of the ring by step 3.1, so multiplying by a trivial factor changes nothing; step 2.1 treats the one-dimensional exact sequences.

Non-split short exact sequences are the degenerate case the proposition must survive; step 2.1 uses exactness of taking weight spaces rather than any splitting, so the additivity is not restricted to direct sums.

boundaries.reason: The proposition concerns short exact sequences and tensor products, with no ordered index or interval whose endpoint could be unverified.

boundaries.evidence: The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the published decomposition and category-O suppliers of [F2] and [F1]; the proposition makes no selection from a varying family itself. The Choice assumption is the one stated in the statement.

boundaries.reason: Additivity and multiplicativity are identities, not a two-way characterisation, so no forward direction of an equivalence is asserted.
The proposition does not claim that every additive function on characters is a tensor product; no reverse iff direction arises.

risk_review.notes: Statement and Proof 1.1–3.1: all finite-dimensional modules have weight decompositions under the stated AC supplier. A weight-preserving surjection is surjective on each weight space by decomposing a lift into weight components. Thus exactness gives coefficientwise addition. The diagonal tensor action and weight-vector bases give the direct sum over mu+nu=eta and its convolution dimension formula. Zero modules and the tensor unit satisfy the formulas. Category O is used for weight-space exactness, not semisimplicity of O. Current item matches post-reader hash.

boundaries.evidence: If Φ is empty, Q+={0}; every cone is a point, so R consists entirely of finite-support series and W={1} acts trivially. The corrected caveat states this exception explicitly. See the Definition statement, Caveat.

The exponent ν=0 is allowed: A(0)=Σw(−1)^ℓ(w)e^0 is the sign-character sum over W, which vanishes as soon as a simple reflection exists and equals e^0 for the trivial group; the definition covers both readings. See the Definition statement, Caveat.

Rank one is the minimal nontrivial case: W={1,s}, the finite-support action sends e^μ to e^{sμ}, and A(ν)=e^ν−e^{sν} consists of two monomials. The case is recorded in the statement. See the Definition statement, Caveat.

Weights fixed by a simple reflection are permitted: the monomials e^{wν} of A(ν) may then collide, and the definition records A(ν) as a coefficient family rather than a set, so the collision is handled by the coefficients. See the Definition statement, Caveat.

boundaries.reason: The definition packages a finite orbit sum; there is no parameter range, boundary index or limiting process whose endpoint could fail.

boundaries.evidence: No choice is exercised: W is finite, the action permutes given monomials, and the caveat is a statement about non-closure of R under W rather than a selection problem. See the Definition statement, Caveat.

No converse is claimed: the definition does not assert that every automorphism of the finite-support part comes from a Weyl element.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module, where $\mathfrak g$ is a
finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra
$\mathfrak h$, and let
$$V=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}V_\mu$$
be its weight-space decomposition, with $V_\mu$ the weight space of
[[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]
([[prop-finite-dimensional-representations-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra-decompose-into-weight-spaces]]).
The **formal character** of $V$ is
$$\operatorname{ch}V:=\sum_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}(\dim V_\mu)e^\mu\in\mathcal R,$$
the finite sum with integer coefficients taken in the completed formal
character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]; equivalently,
$\operatorname{ch}V$ is the coefficient family $\mu\mapsto\dim V_\mu$ on
$\mathfrak h^*$, which has finite support by the cited decomposition.

We write
$$m_\lambda(\mu):=\dim L(\lambda)_\mu$$
for the multiplicity of $\mu$ as a weight of the finite-dimensional simple
module $L(\lambda)$ of highest weight $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$
([[thm-highest-weight-classification-of-finite-dimensional-irreducible-representations]]),
so that $\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=\sum_\mu m_\lambda(\mu)e^\mu$; the
coefficients $m_\lambda(\mu)$ are nonnegative integers and
$m_\lambda(\mu)=0$ for all but finitely many $\mu$.

Let $W$ be the Weyl group of the root system of $\mathfrak g$, acting on
$\mathfrak h^*$ by the root reflections of
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]; by
[[prop-the-weyl-group-is-finite-and-acts-faithfully-on-the-root-system]] and
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]], $W$ is a
finite group and it permutes the roots, hence preserves the root lattice $Q$
and the weight lattice $P$
([[lem-finite-weyl-positive-roots-and-simple-reflections]]).

**Action on finite support.** Every $w\in W$ maps the finite subsets of
$\mathfrak h^*$ to finite subsets, so the assignment $w\cdot e^\mu:=e^{w\mu}$
extends uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-algebra automorphism $f\mapsto w\cdot f$ of
the group ring of finite-support elements of the completed character ring
$\mathcal R$ ([[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]),
with inverse $w^{-1}\cdot(-)$; it restricts to a $\mathbb Z$-algebra
automorphism of $\mathbb Z[P]$, because $W$ preserves the weight lattice $P$.
**Caveat.** If $\Phi\ne\varnothing$, this formula does not define an
action on all of $\mathcal R$. For a simple root $\alpha_i$, the series
$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha_i}$ lies in $\mathcal R$, whereas its image under
$s_i$ has support $\{k\alpha_i:k\ge0\}$, outside every finite union of
downward cones: in each cone the $i$th simple-root coordinate is bounded
above. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, then $Q_+=\{0\}$, every cone is a point,
$\mathcal R$ has only finite-support elements and $W=\{1\}$ acts trivially.
Only finite-support elements are acted on below.

**The alternation operator.** For $\nu\in\mathfrak h^*$ define the **Weyl
alternation operator** by
$$A(\nu):=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\nu},$$
the sum being finite because $W$ is finite; here $\ell$ is the length function
of [[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]] turned into
the sign homomorphism of [[lem-weyl-length-parity-is-multiplicative]]. By
[[lem-weyl-length-parity-is-multiplicative]] the coefficients
$(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ define the determinant sign of $w$ acting on the real span
$E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi$ of the roots. Since the sum is finite,
$A(\nu)$ is a finite-support element of $\mathcal R$ for every $\nu$, and
when $\nu\in P$ it lies in $\mathbb Z[P]\subseteq\mathcal R$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and root system
$\Phi$, choose a positive system $\Phi^+$ with base
$\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\}$
([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]]), let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak g$, and let $W$ be the Weyl
group of $\Phi$, acting on $\mathfrak h^*$ by
complex-linear extension of its action on $E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi$
([[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]],
[[prop-the-roots-form-a-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]).
Then for every simple root $\alpha_i$ and every $\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$
$$\dim V_\mu=\dim V_{s_i(\mu)},\qquad s_i(\mu)=\mu-\mu(h_{\alpha_i})\alpha_i ,$$
and consequently $\dim V_{w\mu}=\dim V_\mu$ for every $w\in W$ and every
$\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]).

Let $\Phi\subseteq E$ be a reduced crystallographic root system with positive
system $\Phi^{+}$, simple roots $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$ and Weyl
group $W$, with inversion sets $N(w)$ and lengths $\ell(w)=|N(w)|$
([[def-length-and-longest-element-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]). Then:
1. for every $w\in W$, the length $\ell(w)$ equals the minimum number of
   simple reflections occurring in an expression of $w$ as a product of simple
   reflections;
2. there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W$; it satisfies
   $w_0(\Phi^{+})=\Phi^{-}$ and $\ell(w_0)=|\Phi^{+}|$.

boundaries.evidence: For V=0 all weight spaces vanish, ch V is the zero series, and the action of any w fixes the zero element; the invariance statement holds with both sides zero.
The zero weight and the zero series are in scope: the coefficient identity dim V_{wμ}=dim V_μ includes μ=0, and step 2.1 records dim V_{w^{-1}ν}=dim V_ν for every ν including ν=0.

The trivial module has a single one-dimensional weight space, fixed by the whole group; more generally one-dimensional weight spaces are covered by the reindexing of step 2.1 without any multiplicity assumption.

Weights with nontrivial stabilisers are admitted: the coefficient identity holds along the entire orbit, and step 2.1 applies the simple-reflection invariance one reflection at a time, so wall weights cause no exception.

boundaries.reason: The statement quantifies over a group and over weights; neither an interval endpoint nor a truncated index set occurs.

boundaries.evidence: The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the published multiplicity supplier of [F3]; the proposition itself performs only a finite reindexing. The Choice assumption is the one stated in the statement.

boundaries.reason: The claim is an invariance identity together with a coefficient restatement, not a biconditional, so there is no forward direction to check.
No converse is asserted: the proposition does not claim that an arbitrary W-invariant family is a character of a finite-dimensional module.

risk_review.notes: Statement and Proof 1.1–3.1: finite character sums can be reindexed, and the opened simple-reflection supplier gives equality of multiplicities for all h* values, including absent weights, with AC stated. Its proof implements each reflection by invertible finite exponentials of the root sl2 operators, with the correct conjugation H -> H-alpha(H)h_alpha; simple generation extends to W. Coefficient comparison proves the asserted equivalence. V=0, trivial representations, singular weights and rank zero are included. Item unchanged pre/post; contract-only enrichment.

Let $\Phi$ be the root system from [[thm-the-root-set-is-a-reduced-crystallographic-root-system]]. For a root $\alpha$, define the corresponding coroot by

$$\alpha^\vee:=\frac{2H_\alpha}{\alpha(H_\alpha)} \in \mathfrak h,$$

where $H_\alpha$ is the vector from [[def-killing-dual-vector-attached-to-a-root]]. The associated **root reflection** is the linear map

$$s_\alpha(\lambda):=\lambda-\lambda(\alpha^\vee)\alpha \qquad (\lambda\in \mathfrak h^*).$$

The subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak h^*)$ generated by these reflections is the **Weyl group** $W$, acting on $\mathfrak h^*$ in the usual way.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. Let $W$ be the Weyl group of the root system of $\mathfrak g$, acting on
$\mathfrak h^*$ by the root reflections of
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]; by
[[prop-the-weyl-group-is-finite-and-acts-faithfully-on-the-root-system]] and
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]], $W$ is a
finite group and it permutes the roots, hence preserves the root lattice $Q$
and the weight lattice $P$
([[lem-finite-weyl-positive-roots-and-simple-reflections]]).

**Action on finite support.** Every $w\in W$ maps the finite subsets of
$\mathfrak h^*$ to finite subsets, so the assignment $w\cdot e^\mu:=e^{w\mu}$
extends uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-algebra automorphism $f\mapsto w\cdot f$ of
the group ring of finite-support elements of the completed character ring
$\mathcal R$ ([[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]),
with inverse $w^{-1}\cdot(-)$; it restricts to a $\mathbb Z$-algebra
automorphism of $\mathbb Z[P]$, because $W$ preserves the weight lattice $P$.
**Caveat.** If $\Phi\ne\varnothing$, this formula does not define an
action on all of $\mathcal R$. For a simple root $\alpha_i$, the series
$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha_i}$ lies in $\mathcal R$, whereas its image under
$s_i$ has support $\{k\alpha_i:k\ge0\}$, outside every finite union of
downward cones: in each cone the $i$th simple-root coordinate is bounded
above. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, then $Q_+=\{0\}$, every cone is a point,
$\mathcal R$ has only finite-support elements and $W=\{1\}$ acts trivially.
Only finite-support elements are acted on below.

**The alternation operator.** For $\nu\in\mathfrak h^*$ define the **Weyl
alternation operator** by
$$A(\nu):=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\nu},$$
the sum being finite because $W$ is finite; here $\ell$ is the length function
of [[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]] turned into
the sign homomorphism of [[lem-weyl-length-parity-is-multiplicative]]. By
[[lem-weyl-length-parity-is-multiplicative]] the coefficients
$(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ define the determinant sign of $w$ acting on the real span
$E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi$ of the roots. Since the sum is finite,
$A(\nu)$ is a finite-support element of $\mathcal R$ for every $\nu$, and
when $\nu\in P$ it lies in $\mathbb Z[P]\subseteq\mathcal R$.

Fix the finite Weyl root-system data of
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]: the real span
$E$ of the roots with its positive definite form, a positive system $\Phi^+$
with base $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, the root group
$Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha\subseteq P$, the weight lattice
$P\subseteq E$, and the positive cone
$$Q_+=\sum_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$$
(the set written $Q^+$ in
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]). A **downward cone**
is a set $\lambda-Q_+=\{\lambda-\beta:\beta\in Q_+\}$ with
$\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$.

The **completed formal character ring** $\mathcal R$ is the set of formal sums
$$f=\sum_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}c_\mu e^\mu,\qquad c_\mu\in\mathbb Z,$$
whose support $\operatorname{supp}f=\{\mu:c_\mu\ne0\}$ is contained in a
finite union of downward cones. Addition is coefficientwise, the product is
the convolution
$$(fg)_\eta=\sum_{\mu+\nu=\eta}c_\mu d_\nu,$$
and the unit is $e^0$, so that $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$. The product is
well defined: if $\operatorname{supp}f$ lies in
$\bigcup_{i=1}^m(\lambda_i-Q_+)$ and $\operatorname{supp}g$ in
$\bigcup_{j=1}^n(\mu_j-Q_+)$, then a pair of exponents contributing to $\eta$
lies in some $\lambda_i-Q_+$ and some $\mu_j-Q_+$, and the solutions
$\beta,\gamma\in Q_+$ of $\beta+\gamma=\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta$ are the elements
of the box $0\le\beta_k\le(\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta)_k$ in the simple-root
coordinates, a finite set (empty unless $\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta\in Q_+$). The
coefficients are integers, and a finite union of downward cones is again such
a union, so addition and multiplication make $\mathcal R$ a commutative
$\mathbb Z$-algebra. In the notation of
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]] this is the ring
denoted $\mathscr R$ there, where the character homomorphism of category
$\mathcal O$ takes its values; the elements of finite support form the group
ring $\mathbb Z[\mathfrak h^*]$ of the additive group $\mathfrak h^*$ and
contain the subring $\mathbb Z[P]$ generated by the $e^\mu$ with
$\mu\in P$.

finite product of elements of $\mathcal R$ lies in $\mathcal R$ by the
convolution formula, while $e^\lambda$ is a single monomial. **No convergence

compared coefficientwise, and every finite sum, product or finite product of
geometric series below is interpreted in $\mathcal R$ by the rules just
recorded.

Fix the finite Weyl root-system data of
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]: the real span
$E$ of the roots with its positive definite form, a positive system $\Phi^+$
with base $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, the root group
$Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha\subseteq P$, the weight lattice
$P\subseteq E$, and the positive cone
$$Q_+=\sum_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$$
(the set written $Q^+$ in
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]). A **downward cone**
is a set $\lambda-Q_+=\{\lambda-\beta:\beta\in Q_+\}$ with
$\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$.

The **completed formal character ring** $\mathcal R$ is the set of formal sums
$$f=\sum_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}c_\mu e^\mu,\qquad c_\mu\in\mathbb Z,$$
whose support $\operatorname{supp}f=\{\mu:c_\mu\ne0\}$ is contained in a
finite union of downward cones. Addition is coefficientwise, the product is
the convolution
$$(fg)_\eta=\sum_{\mu+\nu=\eta}c_\mu d_\nu,$$
and the unit is $e^0$, so that $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$. The product is
well defined: if $\operatorname{supp}f$ lies in
$\bigcup_{i=1}^m(\lambda_i-Q_+)$ and $\operatorname{supp}g$ in
$\bigcup_{j=1}^n(\mu_j-Q_+)$, then a pair of exponents contributing to $\eta$
lies in some $\lambda_i-Q_+$ and some $\mu_j-Q_+$, and the solutions
$\beta,\gamma\in Q_+$ of $\beta+\gamma=\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta$ are the elements
of the box $0\le\beta_k\le(\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta)_k$ in the simple-root
coordinates, a finite set (empty unless $\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta\in Q_+$). The
coefficients are integers, and a finite union of downward cones is again such
a union, so addition and multiplication make $\mathcal R$ a commutative
$\mathbb Z$-algebra. In the notation of
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]] this is the ring
denoted $\mathscr R$ there, where the character homomorphism of category
$\mathcal O$ takes its values; the elements of finite support form the group
ring $\mathbb Z[\mathfrak h^*]$ of the additive group $\mathfrak h^*$ and
contain the subring $\mathbb Z[P]$ generated by the $e^\mu$ with
$\mu\in P$.

By [[prop-formal-character-of-a-verma-module]],
$$\operatorname{ch}M(\lambda)=e^\lambda\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$$
is an element of $\mathcal R$: the geometric series
$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha}$ is supported in the downward cone $-Q_+$, and a
finite product of elements of $\mathcal R$ lies in $\mathcal R$ by the
convolution formula, while $e^\lambda$ is a single monomial. **No convergence
of any formal sum is asserted**: all sums are formal, coefficients are
compared coefficientwise, and every finite sum, product or finite product of
geometric series below is interpreted in $\mathcal R$ by the rules just
recorded.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For the abelian category [[thm-category-o-is-abelian-and-extension-closed]], define $K_0(\mathcal O)$ as the free abelian group on isomorphism classes $[M]$, modulo $[B]=[A]+[C]$ for every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$. A set of representatives suffices: every finitely generated $U(\mathfrak g)$-module is a quotient of some $U(\mathfrak g)^n$, and those quotients form a set up to isomorphism.

Define the formal character by $\operatorname{ch}M=\sum_\mu(\dim M_\mu)e^\mu$. By [[prop-equivalent-support-description-of-category-o]], its integer coefficients are finite and supported in finitely many downward cones. Let $\mathscr R$ be the group of all such integer coefficient families, with pointwise addition. It is a ring with $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$: at a fixed resulting weight, in any pair of cones the equation $\beta+\gamma=\eta$ with $\beta,\gamma\in Q^+$ has finitely many solutions, since every simple-root coefficient is bounded. Taking weight spaces is exact, so character gives a well-defined homomorphism $K_0(\mathcal O)\to\mathscr R$. The zero object's class and character are zero.

system $\Phi^{+}$ and simple roots $\Delta\subseteq\Phi^{+}$
([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]]). Then $\Delta$ is a basis
of $E$; more precisely:
1. $\Delta$ is linearly independent and spans $E$, so $|\Delta|=\dim E$;
2. every positive root is a sum of simple roots with nonnegative integer
   coefficients, and every negative root is a sum of simple roots with
   nonpositive integer coefficients.

Consequently every root is a unique integral combination
$\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}n_\alpha\alpha$ of the simple roots in which the nonzero
coefficients all have the same sign, positive for positive roots and negative
for negative roots.

positive system $\Phi^{+}$ and base $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$ of
simple roots ([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]]). By
[[thm-simple-roots-form-a-basis-and-every-root-has-one-sign-of-integral-coordinates]]
every root is a unique integral combination of $\Delta$ whose nonzero
coefficients all have one sign.

$$\operatorname{ht}(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}n_i .$$
This is well defined because the simple roots form a basis, and simple roots
are exactly the roots of height one. The **root order** on $\Phi$ is defined
by
$$\beta\le\gamma\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \gamma-\beta=\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_i\alpha_i\quad\text{with }m_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.$$
It restricts to a partial order on the positive roots, in which every
comparison chain is finite because heights strictly increase. A positive root
$\theta\in\Phi^{+}$ is a **highest root** if it is maximal for this order,
that is, if $\theta\le\gamma$ for no positive root $\gamma\ne\theta$. The
existence and uniqueness of a highest root for an irreducible system are
proved in [[prop-highest-root-exists-and-is-unique-in-an-irreducible-finite-root-system]].

is an element of $\mathcal R$: the geometric series
$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha}$ is supported in the downward cone $-Q_+$, and a
finite product of elements of $\mathcal R$ lies in $\mathcal R$ by the
convolution formula, while $e^\lambda$ is a single monomial. **No convergence
of any formal sum is asserted**: all sums are formal, coefficients are
compared coefficientwise, and every finite sum, product or finite product of
geometric series below is interpreted in $\mathcal R$ by the rules just
recorded.

Let $\Phi$ be the root system with positive system $\Phi^+$, simple roots
$\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, Weyl group $W$ and Weyl vector
$\rho=\tfrac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha$
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]],
[[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]],
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]). For every $w\in W$,
$$\rho-w\rho=\sum_{\substack{\alpha\in\Phi^+\\ w^{-1}\alpha\in\Phi^-}}\alpha,$$
the sum running over the positive roots whose image under $w^{-1}$ is a
negative root. In particular $\rho-w\rho\in Q_+$: it is a nonnegative integral
combination of the simple roots.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. A **finite reduced crystallographic root system** is a finite subset $\Phi\subseteq E\setminus\{0\}$ spanning $E$, such that for every $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi$ the integer $\langle\beta,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2(\beta,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)$ is integral, the reflection $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ preserves $\Phi$, and the only scalar multiples of $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ are $\alpha,-\alpha$. The **Weyl group** $W$ is the subgroup of linear isometries of $E$ generated by these reflections. A **root reflection** means one of the $s_\alpha$. The empty root system on $E=0$ is allowed, with $W=\{1\}$.

Choose $t\in E$ such that $(t,\alpha)\ne0$ for every root. Put $\Phi^+=\{\alpha:(t,\alpha)>0\}$ and $\Phi^-=-\Phi^+$. A positive root is **simple** if it is not the sum of two positive roots. The following positive-root lemma proves that the simple roots form a basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ and that the simple reflections $s_i=s_{\alpha_i}$ generate $W$; no such assertion is assumed by this definition. Once proved, let $\ell(w)$ be the least number of simple reflections in a word for $w$ and let $\operatorname{Inv}(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi^+:w\alpha\in\Phi^-\}$. A word is reduced if its length equals $\ell(w)$.

Identify $E$ with its dual by the displayed form, so $\alpha^\vee=2\alpha/(\alpha,\alpha)$. The root and coroot groups are $Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha$ and $Q^\vee=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha^\vee$. The **weight group** is $P=\{\lambda\in E:(\lambda,\alpha^\vee)\in\mathbb Z\text{ for all }\alpha\in\Phi\}$; the positive-root lemma proves it is a lattice with basis the vectors dual to the simple coroots. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$. In the Grothendieck group of the linkage block of $\lambda$ ([[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]], [[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]) the finite alternating sum of Verma classes equals the class of the simple module:

$$[L(\lambda)]=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}[M(w\circ\lambda)].$$

Equivalently, applying the character homomorphism and the Verma character $\operatorname{ch}M(\mu)=e^{\mu}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$ ([[prop-formal-character-of-a-verma-module]]),

$$\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\circ\lambda}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1},$$

the Weyl numerator identity in the form needed by the Weyl character formula. Proof: an exact finite complex has vanishing alternating sum of classes.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For the abelian category [[thm-category-o-is-abelian-and-extension-closed]], define $K_0(\mathcal O)$ as the free abelian group on isomorphism classes $[M]$, modulo $[B]=[A]+[C]$ for every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$. A set of representatives suffices: every finitely generated $U(\mathfrak g)$-module is a quotient of some $U(\mathfrak g)^n$, and those quotients form a set up to isomorphism.

Define the formal character by $\operatorname{ch}M=\sum_\mu(\dim M_\mu)e^\mu$. By [[prop-equivalent-support-description-of-category-o]], its integer coefficients are finite and supported in finitely many downward cones. Let $\mathscr R$ be the group of all such integer coefficient families, with pointwise addition. It is a ring with $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$: at a fixed resulting weight, in any pair of cones the equation $\beta+\gamma=\eta$ with $\beta,\gamma\in Q^+$ has finitely many solutions, since every simple-root coefficient is bounded. Taking weight spaces is exact, so character gives a well-defined homomorphism $K_0(\mathcal O)\to\mathscr R$. The zero object's class and character are zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed
positive system. Then the maps
$$V\longmapsto\lambda(V),\qquad \lambda\longmapsto L(\lambda)$$
are mutually inverse bijections between the isomorphism classes of
finite-dimensional irreducible representations of $\mathfrak g$ and the
dominant integral weights
([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]); here $\lambda(V)$
is the highest weight of $V$
([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]) and $L(\lambda)$ is
the simple quotient of $M_{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen
positive system, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional irreducible highest
weight module of highest weight $\lambda$
([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]). Then the
$\lambda$-weight space of $V$ is one-dimensional:
$$\dim V_\lambda=1 .$$

For a vector space $V$ over $k$, write

$$\mathfrak{gl}(V)=\operatorname{End}_k(V)$$

with commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Expansion of triple composites shows
that this is a Lie algebra in every characteristic.

A **representation** of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ on $V$ is a Lie-algebra
homomorphism

$$\rho:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak{gl}(V).$$

Writing $xv$ for $\rho(x)(v)$, this is equivalently a $k$-bilinear action
$\mathfrak g\times V\to V$ satisfying

$$[x,y]v=x(yv)-y(xv)$$

for all $x,y\in\mathfrak g$ and $v\in V$. No finite-dimensional hypothesis is
imposed on either $\mathfrak g$ or $V$. The zero vector space and the zero
action are allowed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module, where $\mathfrak g$ is a
finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra
$\mathfrak h$, and let
$$V=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}V_\mu$$
be its weight-space decomposition, with $V_\mu$ the weight space of
[[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]
([[prop-finite-dimensional-representations-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra-decompose-into-weight-spaces]]).
The **formal character** of $V$ is
$$\operatorname{ch}V:=\sum_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}(\dim V_\mu)e^\mu\in\mathcal R,$$
the finite sum with integer coefficients taken in the completed formal
character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]; equivalently,
$\operatorname{ch}V$ is the coefficient family $\mu\mapsto\dim V_\mu$ on
$\mathfrak h^*$, which has finite support by the cited decomposition.

We write
$$m_\lambda(\mu):=\dim L(\lambda)_\mu$$
for the multiplicity of $\mu$ as a weight of the finite-dimensional simple
module $L(\lambda)$ of highest weight $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$
([[thm-highest-weight-classification-of-finite-dimensional-irreducible-representations]]),
so that $\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=\sum_\mu m_\lambda(\mu)e^\mu$; the
coefficients $m_\lambda(\mu)$ are nonnegative integers and
$m_\lambda(\mu)=0$ for all but finitely many $\mu$.

Let $u\in\mathcal R$ be supported in $-Q_+\setminus\{0\}$, so the
coefficient of $e^0$ in $u$ is $0$ and every exponent in the support of $u$
has strictly negative height, where heights are taken in the simple-root
coordinates of [[def-height-of-a-root-and-highest-root]] and
[[thm-simple-roots-form-a-basis-and-every-root-has-one-sign-of-integral-coordinates]].
Then $1+u$ is invertible in $\mathcal R$, with inverse
$$(1+u)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}(-u)^k,$$
the sum being coefficientwise finite because $u^k$ is supported in weights of
height at most $-k$. In particular:

(i) $e^\mu$ is invertible with inverse $e^{-\mu}$ for every
$\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$;

(ii) the finite product $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})$ equals
$1+u_0$ for an element $u_0$ supported in $-Q_+\setminus\{0\}$, and is
therefore invertible, with
$\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha}$;

(iii) the product $e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})$ is
invertible, with inverse
$e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$;

(iv) for the Weyl vector $\rho$ the alternant $A(\rho)$ of
[[def-weyl-alternation-operator]] factors as
$A(\rho)=e^{\rho}(1+u')$ with $u'$ supported in $-Q_+\setminus\{0\}$, and so
is invertible with inverse $e^{-\rho}(1+u')^{-1}$.

The identification of the inverse in (iv) with the inverse in (iii) is the
content of the Weyl denominator identity proved later and is not asserted
here.

Let $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$ be a dominant integral weight and let $\beta\in\Phi^+$. Then $\langle\lambda+\rho,\beta^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$; in particular $\lambda+\rho$ is regular, so the stabilizer of $\lambda+\rho$ in $W$ is trivial and $w\circ\lambda=w'\circ\lambda$ implies $w=w'$. Moreover the pairing is $W$-invariant: for all $w\in W$, $\langle w(\lambda+\rho),(w\beta)^\vee\rangle=\langle\lambda+\rho,\beta^\vee\rangle$, and $\langle w\circ\lambda+\rho,(w\beta)^\vee\rangle=\langle\lambda+\rho,\beta^\vee\rangle$. Finally every positive coroot is a nonnegative integral combination of the simple coroots, so integrality and positivity are read off on simple coroots and extended by $W$-invariance.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen
positive system whose base is the set of simple roots
$\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$
([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]],
[[prop-the-roots-form-a-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]).
For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ write
$$\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle:=\lambda(h_{\alpha_i})$$
for the pairing with the simple coroots
([[def-coroot-of-a-lie-algebra-root]]). Then $\lambda$ is:

* **integral** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ for every $i$;
* **dominant integral** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for every $i$;
* **strictly dominant** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle>0$ for every $i$;
* **antidominant** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\le0$ for every $i$.

Dominance, strict dominance, and antidominance depend on the chosen base
$\Delta$ and hence on the positive system: the same functional may be dominant
for one choice and antidominant for another. Integrality is independent of that
choice, because, as verified below, it is exactly membership in the weight
lattice $P$. Only the integer and the sign of the finitely many simple-coroot
pairings enter the displayed tests, so they are finite verifications.

**Integral weights are the weight lattice.** By
[[thm-simple-roots-form-a-basis-and-every-root-has-one-sign-of-integral-coordinates]]
and step (v) of
[[prop-the-roots-form-a-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]] the
simple roots form a basis of $E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi$ and the
simple coroots form a basis of $\mathfrak h$, so a functional
$\lambda\in E$ is determined by its pairings with the simple coroots. The
fundamental weights $\omega_1,\dots,\omega_r$ are dual to the simple coroots,
$(\omega_i,\alpha_j^\vee)=\delta_{ij}$
([[def-fundamental-weights]]), and they form a basis of the weight lattice
$P$ ([[def-root-lattice-coroot-lattice-weight-lattice-and-coweight-lattice]]).
Hence every $\lambda\in E$ has the unique expansion
$$\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^r\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\,\omega_i ,$$
so for $\lambda\in E$ integrality is equivalent to $\lambda\in P$. Conversely
an integral $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ automatically lies in $E$: the simple
coroots form a real basis of $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ by loc. cit., the values
$\lambda(h_{\alpha_i})$ are real, hence $\lambda$ is real valued on
$\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$, which is exactly the condition defining $E$ inside
$\mathfrak h^*$. Thus the integral weights are the elements of $P\subseteq E$,
and the dominant integral weights are those elements of $P$ whose
fundamental-weight coefficients are nonnegative integers.  By contrast, the
strictly dominant weights are all elements of $E$ whose fundamental-weight
coefficients are positive real numbers; they need not be integral or belong to
$P$.

For the preceding finite reduced crystallographic root system, regular vectors $t$ exist, $W$ is finite, and the simple positive roots are a basis of $E$. Every root has integral coordinates in this basis of one sign. Each $s_i$ permutes $\Phi^+\setminus\{\alpha_i\}$ and sends $\alpha_i$ to $-\alpha_i$. The simple reflections generate $W$, and every root is the image of a simple root under their group. The simple coroots similarly form an integral basis of the coroot group, and $P$ is the lattice generated by their dual basis; $W$ preserves $Q,Q^\vee,P$. All assertions are choice-free, including rank zero.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. A **finite reduced crystallographic root system** is a finite subset $\Phi\subseteq E\setminus\{0\}$ spanning $E$, such that for every $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi$ the integer $\langle\beta,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2(\beta,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)$ is integral, the reflection $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ preserves $\Phi$, and the only scalar multiples of $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ are $\alpha,-\alpha$. The **Weyl group** $W$ is the subgroup of linear isometries of $E$ generated by these reflections. A **root reflection** means one of the $s_\alpha$. The empty root system on $E=0$ is allowed, with $W=\{1\}$.

Choose $t\in E$ such that $(t,\alpha)\ne0$ for every root. Put $\Phi^+=\{\alpha:(t,\alpha)>0\}$ and $\Phi^-=-\Phi^+$. A positive root is **simple** if it is not the sum of two positive roots. The following positive-root lemma proves that the simple roots form a basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ and that the simple reflections $s_i=s_{\alpha_i}$ generate $W$; no such assertion is assumed by this definition. Once proved, let $\ell(w)$ be the least number of simple reflections in a word for $w$ and let $\operatorname{Inv}(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi^+:w\alpha\in\Phi^-\}$. A word is reduced if its length equals $\ell(w)$.

Identify $E$ with its dual by the displayed form, so $\alpha^\vee=2\alpha/(\alpha,\alpha)$. The root and coroot groups are $Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha$ and $Q^\vee=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha^\vee$. The **weight group** is $P=\{\lambda\in E:(\lambda,\alpha^\vee)\in\mathbb Z\text{ for all }\alpha\in\Phi\}$; the positive-root lemma proves it is a lattice with basis the vectors dual to the simple coroots. Put $Q_+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$, and write $\mu\le\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q_+$. The open and closed positive chambers are $\mathcal C=\{x:(x,\alpha_i)>0\text{ for all }i\}$ and $\overline{\mathcal C}=\{x:(x,\alpha_i)\ge0\text{ for all }i\}$. A weight is dominant if it belongs to $P\cap\overline{\mathcal C}$. More generally chambers are the connected components of $E\setminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\alpha^\perp$. The closed-chamber representative and stabilizer assertions are proved later, not included as axioms.

Let $W$ be the Weyl group of the root system of $\mathfrak g$, acting on
$\mathfrak h^*$ by the root reflections of
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]; by
[[prop-the-weyl-group-is-finite-and-acts-faithfully-on-the-root-system]] and
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]], $W$ is a
finite group and it permutes the roots, hence preserves the root lattice $Q$
and the weight lattice $P$
([[lem-finite-weyl-positive-roots-and-simple-reflections]]).

**Action on finite support.** Every $w\in W$ maps the finite subsets of
$\mathfrak h^*$ to finite subsets, so the assignment $w\cdot e^\mu:=e^{w\mu}$
extends uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-algebra automorphism $f\mapsto w\cdot f$ of
the group ring of finite-support elements of the completed character ring
$\mathcal R$ ([[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]),
with inverse $w^{-1}\cdot(-)$; it restricts to a $\mathbb Z$-algebra
automorphism of $\mathbb Z[P]$, because $W$ preserves the weight lattice $P$.
**Caveat.** If $\Phi\ne\varnothing$, this formula does not define an
action on all of $\mathcal R$. For a simple root $\alpha_i$, the series
$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha_i}$ lies in $\mathcal R$, whereas its image under
$s_i$ has support $\{k\alpha_i:k\ge0\}$, outside every finite union of
downward cones: in each cone the $i$th simple-root coordinate is bounded
above. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, then $Q_+=\{0\}$, every cone is a point,
$\mathcal R$ has only finite-support elements and $W=\{1\}$ acts trivially.
Only finite-support elements are acted on below.

**The alternation operator.** For $\nu\in\mathfrak h^*$ define the **Weyl
alternation operator** by
$$A(\nu):=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\nu},$$
the sum being finite because $W$ is finite; here $\ell$ is the length function
of [[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]] turned into
the sign homomorphism of [[lem-weyl-length-parity-is-multiplicative]]. By
[[lem-weyl-length-parity-is-multiplicative]] the coefficients
$(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ define the determinant sign of $w$ acting on the real span
$E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi$ of the roots. Since the sum is finite,
$A(\nu)$ is a finite-support element of $\mathcal R$ for every $\nu$, and
when $\nu\in P$ it lies in $\mathbb Z[P]\subseteq\mathcal R$.

Fix the finite Weyl root-system data of
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]: the real span
$E$ of the roots with its positive definite form, a positive system $\Phi^+$
with base $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, the root group
$Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha\subseteq P$, the weight lattice
$P\subseteq E$, and the positive cone
$$Q_+=\sum_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$$
(the set written $Q^+$ in
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]). A **downward cone**
is a set $\lambda-Q_+=\{\lambda-\beta:\beta\in Q_+\}$ with
$\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$.

The **completed formal character ring** $\mathcal R$ is the set of formal sums
$$f=\sum_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}c_\mu e^\mu,\qquad c_\mu\in\mathbb Z,$$
whose support $\operatorname{supp}f=\{\mu:c_\mu\ne0\}$ is contained in a
finite union of downward cones. Addition is coefficientwise, the product is
the convolution
$$(fg)_\eta=\sum_{\mu+\nu=\eta}c_\mu d_\nu,$$
and the unit is $e^0$, so that $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$. The product is
well defined: if $\operatorname{supp}f$ lies in
$\bigcup_{i=1}^m(\lambda_i-Q_+)$ and $\operatorname{supp}g$ in
$\bigcup_{j=1}^n(\mu_j-Q_+)$, then a pair of exponents contributing to $\eta$
lies in some $\lambda_i-Q_+$ and some $\mu_j-Q_+$, and the solutions
$\beta,\gamma\in Q_+$ of $\beta+\gamma=\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta$ are the elements
of the box $0\le\beta_k\le(\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta)_k$ in the simple-root
coordinates, a finite set (empty unless $\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta\in Q_+$). The
coefficients are integers, and a finite union of downward cones is again such
a union, so addition and multiplication make $\mathcal R$ a commutative
$\mathbb Z$-algebra. In the notation of
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]] this is the ring
denoted $\mathscr R$ there, where the character homomorphism of category
$\mathcal O$ takes its values; the elements of finite support form the group
ring $\mathbb Z[\mathfrak h^*]$ of the additive group $\mathfrak h^*$ and
contain the subring $\mathbb Z[P]$ generated by the $e^\mu$ with
$\mu\in P$.

By [[prop-formal-character-of-a-verma-module]],
$$\operatorname{ch}M(\lambda)=e^\lambda\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$$
is an element of $\mathcal R$: the geometric series
$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha}$ is supported in the downward cone $-Q_+$, and a
finite product of elements of $\mathcal R$ lies in $\mathcal R$ by the
convolution formula, while $e^\lambda$ is a single monomial. **No convergence
of any formal sum is asserted**: all sums are formal, coefficients are
compared coefficientwise, and every finite sum, product or finite product of
geometric series below is interpreted in $\mathcal R$ by the rules just
recorded.

derivations.claim: The Euler identity [F1] at the dominant integral weight $\lambda=0$ reads $\operatorname{ch}L(0)=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\rho-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$, and [F2] gives $\operatorname{ch}L(0)=1=e^0$.

Multiplying both sides of step 1.1 by the invertible element $e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})$ of [F3] and cancelling the inverse against the product yields $e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\rho-\rho+\rho}=A(\rho)$, which is the first form of the identity.

For the half-root form, expand each factor using [F5]: $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(e^{\alpha/2}-e^{-\alpha/2})=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}e^{-\alpha/2}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(e^{\alpha}-1)=e^{-\rho}(-1)^{|\Phi^+|}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{\alpha})=e^{-\rho}(-1)^{|\Phi^+|}(-1)^{|\Phi^+|}e^{2\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})=e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})$, using $1-e^{\alpha}=-e^{\alpha}(1-e^{-\alpha})$ and $\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha=2\rho$; with step 2.1 this equals $A(\rho)$.

All exponents in $A(\rho)$ are the $w\rho$, and all exponents in the expanded right side are $\rho$ minus sums of positive roots; both lie in $P$ by [F4], so the identity of steps 2.1 and 3.1 is an identity in $\mathbb Z[P]$, and since $A(\rho)$ equals the invertible element of [F3], it is invertible with the stated inverse.

boundaries.evidence: Empty root system: W={1}, ρ=0, both sides equal e^0 and the finite sum and product are one-term; step 2.1 then reads e^0=e^0.
The trivial weight λ=0 feeds step 1.1 with ch L(0)=e^0; the exponent w∘0 may be zero, and no division by a vanishing quantity occurs because only the invertibility of the product is used.
Rank one: the identity reads e^ω−e^{−ω}=e^ω(1−e^{−α}) with α=2ω, a single-factor product, as computed in step 3.1.

Wall phenomena do not degenerate the left side: wρ is always regular because ρ is strictly dominant, so the |W| monomials are distinct and the sum has no cancellations beyond the signs; step 4.1 only uses wρ∈P.

boundaries.reason: Both sides are finite expressions in a group ring; no convergence parameter or boundary of an interval is involved.

boundaries.evidence: The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the BGG Euler identity of step 1.1; the remaining inputs are a finite sum over W and a finite product over Φ+, requiring no choice.

boundaries.reason: The theorem states an identity between two finite expressions; it is not a biconditional, so no forward direction exists.
No converse is claimed: the theorem does not say that any element equal to the product form must be a Weyl alternant.

risk_review.notes: Statement and Proof 1.1–4.1: BGG Euler character at dominant lambda=0 and the one-dimensional trivial module give 1=e^{-rho}A(rho)G. Multiply by the verified root product unit to obtain A(rho)=e^rho product(1-e^{-alpha}); the half-root factorization is computed with both (-1)^|Phi+| signs cancelling. Although individual alpha/2 factors need not lie in P, their expanded exponents rho minus root sums do, so the identity is in Z[P] and the inverse only in the completion. Rank zero gives 1=1. Opened the full Euler supplier and its BGG resolution, plus the kernel-dimension, coinvariant-injection and graded-surjectivity proofs; the exactness induction has the stated degree hypotheses and no use of the Weyl character formula. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$. In the Grothendieck group of the linkage block of $\lambda$ ([[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]], [[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]) the finite alternating sum of Verma classes equals the class of the simple module:

$$[L(\lambda)]=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}[M(w\circ\lambda)].$$

Equivalently, applying the character homomorphism and the Verma character $\operatorname{ch}M(\mu)=e^{\mu}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$ ([[prop-formal-character-of-a-verma-module]]),

$$\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\circ\lambda}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1},$$

the Weyl numerator identity in the form needed by the Weyl character formula. Proof: an exact finite complex has vanishing alternating sum of classes.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For the abelian category [[thm-category-o-is-abelian-and-extension-closed]], define $K_0(\mathcal O)$ as the free abelian group on isomorphism classes $[M]$, modulo $[B]=[A]+[C]$ for every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$. A set of representatives suffices: every finitely generated $U(\mathfrak g)$-module is a quotient of some $U(\mathfrak g)^n$, and those quotients form a set up to isomorphism.

Define the formal character by $\operatorname{ch}M=\sum_\mu(\dim M_\mu)e^\mu$. By [[prop-equivalent-support-description-of-category-o]], its integer coefficients are finite and supported in finitely many downward cones. Let $\mathscr R$ be the group of all such integer coefficient families, with pointwise addition. It is a ring with $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$: at a fixed resulting weight, in any pair of cones the equation $\beta+\gamma=\eta$ with $\beta,\gamma\in Q^+$ has finitely many solutions, since every simple-root coefficient is bounded. Taking weight spaces is exact, so character gives a well-defined homomorphism $K_0(\mathcal O)\to\mathscr R$. The zero object's class and character are zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). In the completed
character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]],
$$A(\rho)=e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha});$$
equivalently
$$\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\rho}=e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\rho}=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\bigl(e^{\alpha/2}-e^{-\alpha/2}\bigr),$$
where $\rho=\tfrac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha$ is the Weyl vector
([[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]]) and $A(\rho)$ is the
alternant of [[def-weyl-alternation-operator]]. Both sides are finite
expressions: the left side is a finite sum and the right side is a finite
product, and the identity holds in the group ring $\mathbb Z[P]$.
Consequently $A(\rho)$ is invertible, with
$$A(\rho)^{-1}=e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}.$$

Let $u\in\mathcal R$ be supported in $-Q_+\setminus\{0\}$, so the
coefficient of $e^0$ in $u$ is $0$ and every exponent in the support of $u$
has strictly negative height, where heights are taken in the simple-root
coordinates of [[def-height-of-a-root-and-highest-root]] and
[[thm-simple-roots-form-a-basis-and-every-root-has-one-sign-of-integral-coordinates]].
Then $1+u$ is invertible in $\mathcal R$, with inverse
$$(1+u)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}(-u)^k,$$
the sum being coefficientwise finite because $u^k$ is supported in weights of
height at most $-k$. In particular:

(i) $e^\mu$ is invertible with inverse $e^{-\mu}$ for every
$\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$;

(ii) the finite product $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})$ equals
$1+u_0$ for an element $u_0$ supported in $-Q_+\setminus\{0\}$, and is
therefore invertible, with
$\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha}$;

(iii) the product $e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})$ is
invertible, with inverse
$e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$;

(iv) for the Weyl vector $\rho$ the alternant $A(\rho)$ of
[[def-weyl-alternation-operator]] factors as
$A(\rho)=e^{\rho}(1+u')$ with $u'$ supported in $-Q_+\setminus\{0\}$, and so
is invertible with inverse $e^{-\rho}(1+u')^{-1}$.

The identification of the inverse in (iv) with the inverse in (iii) is the
content of the Weyl denominator identity proved later and is not asserted
here.

Let $W$ be the Weyl group of the root system of $\mathfrak g$, acting on
$\mathfrak h^*$ by the root reflections of
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]; by
[[prop-the-weyl-group-is-finite-and-acts-faithfully-on-the-root-system]] and
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]], $W$ is a
finite group and it permutes the roots, hence preserves the root lattice $Q$

extends uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-algebra automorphism $f\mapsto w\cdot f$ of

$\mathcal R$ ([[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]),
with inverse $w^{-1}\cdot(-)$; it restricts to a $\mathbb Z$-algebra

**The alternation operator.** For $\nu\in\mathfrak h^*$ define the **Weyl

$$A(\nu):=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\nu},$$
the sum being finite because $W$ is finite; here $\ell$ is the length function
of [[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]] turned into

[[lem-weyl-length-parity-is-multiplicative]] the coefficients

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module, where $\mathfrak g$ is a
finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra
$\mathfrak h$, and let
$$V=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}V_\mu$$
be its weight-space decomposition, with $V_\mu$ the weight space of
[[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]
([[prop-finite-dimensional-representations-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra-decompose-into-weight-spaces]]).
The **formal character** of $V$ is
$$\operatorname{ch}V:=\sum_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}(\dim V_\mu)e^\mu\in\mathcal R,$$
the finite sum with integer coefficients taken in the completed formal
character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]; equivalently,
$\operatorname{ch}V$ is the coefficient family $\mu\mapsto\dim V_\mu$ on
$\mathfrak h^*$, which has finite support by the cited decomposition.

We write
$$m_\lambda(\mu):=\dim L(\lambda)_\mu$$
for the multiplicity of $\mu$ as a weight of the finite-dimensional simple
module $L(\lambda)$ of highest weight $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$
([[thm-highest-weight-classification-of-finite-dimensional-irreducible-representations]]),
so that $\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=\sum_\mu m_\lambda(\mu)e^\mu$; the
coefficients $m_\lambda(\mu)$ are nonnegative integers and
$m_\lambda(\mu)=0$ for all but finitely many $\mu$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen
positive system whose base is the set of simple roots
$\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$
([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]],
[[prop-the-roots-form-a-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]).
For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ write
$$\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle:=\lambda(h_{\alpha_i})$$
for the pairing with the simple coroots
([[def-coroot-of-a-lie-algebra-root]]). Then $\lambda$ is:

* **integral** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ for every $i$;
* **dominant integral** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for every $i$;
* **strictly dominant** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle>0$ for every $i$;
* **antidominant** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\le0$ for every $i$.

Dominance, strict dominance, and antidominance depend on the chosen base

choice, because, as verified below, it is exactly membership in the weight
lattice $P$. Only the integer and the sign of the finitely many simple-coroot
pairings enter the displayed tests, so they are finite verifications.

**Integral weights are the weight lattice.** By
[[thm-simple-roots-form-a-basis-and-every-root-has-one-sign-of-integral-coordinates]]
and step (v) of
[[prop-the-roots-form-a-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]] the
simple roots form a basis of $E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi$ and the
simple coroots form a basis of $\mathfrak h$, so a functional
$\lambda\in E$ is determined by its pairings with the simple coroots. The

$(\omega_i,\alpha_j^\vee)=\delta_{ij}$
([[def-fundamental-weights]]), and they form a basis of the weight lattice
$P$ ([[def-root-lattice-coroot-lattice-weight-lattice-and-coweight-lattice]]).
Hence every $\lambda\in E$ has the unique expansion
$$\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^r\langle\lambda,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\,\omega_i ,$$
so for $\lambda\in E$ integrality is equivalent to $\lambda\in P$. Conversely
an integral $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ automatically lies in $E$: the simple
coroots form a real basis of $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ by loc. cit., the values
$\lambda(h_{\alpha_i})$ are real, hence $\lambda$ is real valued on
$\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$, which is exactly the condition defining $E$ inside
$\mathfrak h^*$. Thus the integral weights are the elements of $P\subseteq E$,
and the dominant integral weights are those elements of $P$ whose
fundamental-weight coefficients are nonnegative integers.  By contrast, the
strictly dominant weights are all elements of $E$ whose fundamental-weight
coefficients are positive real numbers; they need not be integral or belong to
$P$.

$$\rho:=\frac12\sum_{\alpha\in \Phi^+} \alpha \in \mathfrak h^*.$$

This is the shift used in the dot action and in the quadratic Casimir eigenvalue formula on this page.
